Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe wicked reign of Jehoram.1–11Jehoram's miserable end.12–20
Jehoram's wicked reign (verses 1–11)

Jehoram hated his brothers and killed them for the same reason Cain hated and killed Abel: their godliness condemned his ungodliness.

In the mysterious workings of Providence, such wicked people sometimes prosper for a time.

Yet God has righteous reasons for permitting those events.

We can understand some of those purposes now; the rest will become clear in the future.

Jehoram's miserable death (verses 12–20)

God sent Jehoram a warning.

The Spirit of prophecy may have directed Elijah to write it in advance, foreseeing Jehoram's crimes.

Jehoram was told plainly that his sins would bring ruin.

It is no surprise that sinners ignore warnings of punishment in the world to come, when even the certainty of suffering in this life—losing possessions or health—does not make them abandon wicked practices.

Jehoram lost every comfort.

God made clear that he was confronting both the king and his household.

Jehoram had killed his brothers to make himself secure.

Now all but one of his sons were killed.

Yet David's family would not be destroyed entirely as many northern royal families were, because the promise of the Messiah belonged to David's line.

Good people may also suffer disease, but for them illness is fatherly correction.

God's comfort can keep the soul at rest even while the body is in pain.

To be ill and poor or ill and lonely is distressing.

But to be ill while living in sin, under God's judgment and without grace to endure it is far more terrible.

Wickedness and irreverence make people contemptible even to those with little religion themselves.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.21.1-2Chr.21.11]
Chapter 21
Chapter Outline
The wicked reign of Jehoram. | (1-11) |
Jehoram's miserable end. | (12-20) |
Verses 1-11
Jehoram hated his brethren, and slew them, for the same reason that Cain hated Abel, and slew him, because their piety condemned his impiety. In the mystery of Providence such men sometimes prosper for a time; but the Lord has righteous purposes in permitting such events, part of which may now be made out, and the rest will be seen hereafter.
[2Chr.21.12-2Chr.21.20]
Verses 12-20
A warning from God was sent to Jehoram. The Spirit of prophecy might direct Elijah to prepare this writing in the foresight of Jehoram's crimes. He is plainly told that his sin should certainly ruin him. But no marvel that sinners are not frightened from sin, and to repentance, by the threatenings of misery in another world, when the certainty of misery in this world, the sinking of their estates, and the ruin of their health, will not restrain them from vicious courses. See Jehoram here stripped of all his comforts. Thus God plainly showed that the controversy was with him, and his house. He had slain all his brethren to strengthen himself; now, all his sons are slain but one. David's house must not be wholly destroyed, like those of Israel's kings, because a blessing was in it; that of the Messiah. Good men may be afflicted with diseases; but to them they are fatherly chastisements, and by the support of Divine consolations the soul may dwell at ease, even when the body lies in pain. To be sick and poor, sick and solitary, but especially to be sick and in sin, sick and under the curse of God, sick and without grace to bear it, is a most deplorable case. Wickedness and profaneness make men despicable, even in the eyes of those who have but little religion.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The reign of Ahaziah, Athaliah destroys the royal family.

Ahaziah's reign and Athaliah's attempt to destroy David's line

The counsel of wicked people ruins many young people as they begin adult life.

Ahaziah allowed himself to be led by evil advisers.

People who encourage us to do wrong are advising us toward our destruction.

Though they pretend to be friends, they are our worst enemies.

Consider the harm caused by bad company.

Even when we escape being infected by its wickedness, we should still fear sharing its destruction (Revelation 18:4).

Here a wicked woman tried to destroy David's house, while a good woman preserved it.

Not one word of God's promise will fail.

At this point the prophecies that the Messiah would descend from David—and thus the salvation of the world—seemed to depend upon the fragile life of a single infant.

The ruling power wanted that child dead.

But God had made his purpose known, and the efforts of earth and hell could not defeat it.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.22.1]
Chapter 22
The reign of Ahaziah, Athaliah destroys the royal family.
--The counsel of the ungodly ruins many young persons when they are setting out in the world. Ahaziah gave himself up to be led by evil men. Those who advise us to do wickedly, counsel us to our destruction; while they pretend to be friends, they are our worst enemies. See and dread the mischief of bad company. If not the infection, yet let the destruction be feared, [Rev.18.4] Re 18:4. We have here, a wicked woman endeavouring to destroy the house of David, and a good woman preserving it. No word of God shall fall to the ground. The whole truth of the prophecies that the Messiah was to come from David, and thereby the salvation of the world, appeared to be now hung upon the brittle thread of the life of a single infant, to destroy whom was the interest of the reigning power. But God had purposed, and vain were the efforts of earth and hell.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Joash crowned, and Athaliah slain.

Joash becomes king

Recognizing ourselves and one another as the Lord's people should make us earnest in carrying out our duties both toward God and toward other human beings.

In this way the change of government was accomplished successfully, and the people rejoiced.

When the Son of David is enthroned within a person's soul, peace and joy follow.

For the related account, see 2 Kings 11.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.23.1]
Chapter 23
Joash crowned, and Athaliah slain.
--To look upon ourselves and each other as the Lord's people, should make us earnest in the discharge of our duty both to God and man. Thus was this happy revolution brought about, and the people rejoiced. When the Son of David is enthroned in the soul, all is quiet, and joyful. See 2Ki 11.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJoash, of Judah, The temple repaired.1–14Joash falls into idolatry, He is slain by his servants.15–27
Joash repairs the temple (verses 1–14)

Joash showed even greater zeal for repairing the temple than Jehoiada did.

Yet it is easier to build or repair a temple than to become a temple of God oneself.

Repairing places used for public worship is still a good work that everyone should help advance.

Many worthy projects remain unfinished simply because no energetic person takes responsibility for moving them forward.

Joash abandons God and is killed (verses 15–27)

The death of a faithful, zealous and useful servant of God can be a great judgment on a ruler or people.

This shows why our faith must spring from an inward principle, not depend entirely on the presence of another human being.

Otherwise, when a parent, minister or friend dies, we may lose our religion along with that person.

Rulers and ordinary people alike have often been flattered into ruin.

Only genuine grace enables a person to keep bearing spiritual fruit until the end.

Zechariah, Jehoiada's son, stood up in the Spirit of prophecy and exposed the people's sin.

That is the task of ministers: using God's word like a lamp, they reveal wrongdoing and explain the meaning of divine Providence.

The people stoned Zechariah to death in the temple court.

As he died, he called upon the Lord to see and require judgment for the crime.

Henry says this was not a cry of private revenge but a prophetic declaration.

God struck Joash with severe illness, whether in body, mind or both, before the Syrians left.

When judgment pursues sinners, the end of one trouble may simply introduce another.

Joash's own servants killed him.

The judgments were described as burdens because God's wrath is a load too heavy for any person to bear.

May God help us learn from the warning, remain upright in heart and persevere in his ways until the end.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.24.1-2Chr.24.14]
Chapter 24
Chapter Outline
Joash, of Judah, The temple repaired. | (1-14) |
Joash falls into idolatry, He is slain by his servants. | (15-27) |
Verses 1-14
Joash is more zealous about the repair of the temple than Jehoiada himself. It is easier to build temples, than to be temples to God. But the repairing of places for public worship is a good work, which all should promote. And many a good work would be done that now lies undone, if active men would put it forward.
[2Chr.24.15-2Chr.24.27]
Verses 15-27
See what a great judgment on any prince or people, the death of godly, zealous, useful men is. See how necessary it is that we act in religion from inward principle. Then the loss of a parent, a minister, or a friend, will not be losing our religion. Often both princes and inferior people have been flattered to their ruin. True grace alone will enable a man to bring forth fruit unto the end. Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada, being filled with the Spirit of prophecy, stood up, and told the people of their sin. This is the work of ministers, by the word of God, as a lamp and a light, to discover the sin of men, and expound the providences of God. They stoned Zechariah to death in the court of the house of the Lord. Observe the dying martyr's words: The Lord look upon it, and require it! This came not from a spirit of revenge, but a spirit of prophecy. God smote Joash with great diseases, of body, or mind, or both, before the Syrians departed from him. If vengeance pursue men, the end of one trouble will be but the beginning of another. His own servants slew him. These judgments are called the burdens laid upon him, for the wrath of God is a heavy burden, too heavy for any man to bear. May God help us to take warning, to be upright in heart, and to persevere in his ways to the end.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesAmaziah, king of Judah.1–13Amaziah worships the idols of Edom.14–16Amaziah's rash challenge.17–28
Amaziah's reign begins (verses 1–13)

Amaziah was not an enemy of true religion, but he was a lukewarm and indifferent friend.

Many people do what is right without doing it with their whole hearts.

Rash decisions create painful work for repentance.

Yet Amaziah deserved honor for obeying God's command when it required sacrifice.

A firm belief that God is fully able to uphold us in duty and make up for losses suffered in serving him makes his commands easier to bear.

When we must surrender something for God and his worship, we can be content knowing he can provide something much better.

Sinners who have been convinced intellectually but do not possess genuine faith often object when obedience requires self-denial.

Like Amaziah, they ask, “But what shall we do about the hundred talents?”

What if keeping the Sabbath means losing good customers?

What if obedience costs a profitable business opportunity or the world's friendship?

People often try to quiet their consciences by claiming that forbidden practices are necessary.

The answer remains the same: the Lord can give you far more than that.

Even in this life, he can make up for what is surrendered for his sake.

Amaziah worships Edom's idols (verses 14–16)

After defeating the Edomites, Amaziah worshiped the gods who had failed to protect the people he conquered.

What absurdity!

If people seriously considered how powerless the things they turn to are, they would not abandon the Lord and harm themselves.

The prophet's rebuke was so just that Amaziah could not answer it, except by ordering the prophet to stop speaking.

Sinners may feel relieved when they silence those correcting them.

But people who refuse to hear correction are becoming ready for destruction.

Amaziah challenges Israel and is humiliated (verses 17–28)

Few proud rulers have been more completely humbled than Amaziah by Jehoash, king of Israel.

Pride brings a person low (Proverbs 29:23).

It goes before destruction and rightly produces it.

Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.

Someone who rushes into a quarrel may find himself humiliated and at a loss when his opponent answers him (Proverbs 25:8).

What are we when we try to establish our own righteousness or justify ourselves before the Most High God?

We resemble contemptible thistles imagining themselves majestic cedars.

Temptations and sinful desires are like wild beasts that trample such proud pretensions into the dust.

A person's destruction can often be traced to the moment the person turned away from the Lord.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.25.1-2Chr.25.13]
Chapter 25
Chapter Outline
Amaziah, king of Judah. | (1-13) |
Amaziah worships the idols of Edom. | (14-16) |
Amaziah's rash challenge. | (17-28) |
Verses 1-13
Amaziah was no enemy to religion, but cool and indifferent friend. Many do what is good, but not with a perfect heart. Rashness makes work for repentance. But Amaziah's obedience to the command of God was to his honour. A firm belief of God's all-sufficiency to bear us out in our duty, and to make up all the loss and damage we sustain in his service, will make his yoke very easy, and his burden very light. When we are called to part with any thing for God and our religion, it should satisfy us, that God is able to give us much more than this. Convinced sinners, who have not true faith, always object to self-denying obedience. They are like Amaziah; they say, But what shall we do for the hundred talents? What shall we do if by keeping the sabbath holy we lose so many good customers? What shall we do without this gain? What shall we do if we lose the friendship of the world? Many endeavour to quiet their consciences by the pretence that forbidden practices are necessary. The answer is, as here, The Lord is able to give thee much more than this. He makes up, even in this world, for all that is given up for his sake.
[2Chr.25.14-2Chr.25.16]
Verses 14-16
To worship the gods of those whom Amaziah had conquered, who could not help their own worshippers, was the greatest absurdity. If men would consider how unable all those things are to help them, to which they look whenever they forsake God, they would not be such enemies to themselves. The reproof God sent by a prophet was too just to be answered; but he was bidden not to say a word more. The secure sinner rejoices to have silenced his reprovers and monitors; but what comes of it? Those that are deaf to reproof, are ripening for destruction.
[2Chr.25.17-2Chr.25.28]
Verses 17-28
Never was a proud prince more thoroughly mortified than Amaziah by Joash king of Israel. A man's pride will bring him low, [Prov.29.23] Pr 29:23; it goes before his destruction, and deservedly brings it on. He that exalteth himself shall be abased. He that goes forth hastily to strive, will not know what he shall do in the end thereof, when his neighbour has put him to shame, [Prov.25.8] Pr 25:8. And what are we when we offer to establish our own righteousness, or presume to justify ourselves before the Most High God, but despicable thistles, that fancy themselves stately cedars? And are not various temptations, is not every corruption, a wild beast of the desert, which will trample on the wretched boaster, and tread his haughty pretensions to the dust? A man's pride shall bring him low; his ruin may be dated from his turning from the Lord.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesUzziah's good reign in Judah.1–15Uzziah's attempt to burn incense.16–23
Uzziah's prosperous reign (verses 1–15)

As long as Uzziah sought the Lord and paid attention to true religion, God made him prosper.

Only those whom God makes prosperous truly prosper, because success comes from him.

Many people can testify that they prospered while they sought God and attended to their duties, but difficulties multiplied when they turned away.

God does not continually bless laziness or withhold his blessing from diligence.

No one who sincerely seeks him does so in vain.

Uzziah became famous throughout the neighboring countries.

Having a good reputation before God and godly people is true honor.

He did not delight in warfare or excessive amusement, but loved agriculture.

Uzziah tries to burn incense (verses 16–23)

Earlier kings had sinned by abandoning God's temple and burning incense at idolatrous altars.

Uzziah's sin was different: he entered God's sanctuary and tried to burn incense on God's own altar.

How difficult it is to avoid one extreme without falling into the opposite!

Pride lay at the root of his wrongdoing.

Instead of lifting up God's name in gratitude for everything he had received, Uzziah lifted up his own heart to his own harm.

The desire for forbidden knowledge and honors beyond one's proper place often comes from pride.

Our prayers, like incense, must be placed by faith into the hands of Jesus Christ our great High Priest, or we cannot expect God to accept them (Revelation 8:3).

Uzziah argued with the priests but could not prevail against his Creator.

He was afflicted with leprosy and lived apart from society until death.

His punishment corresponded to his sin.

Because he sought unlawful honor, God humbled and disgraced him.

Those who covet forbidden honors may lose the honors lawfully available to them.

Adam reached for knowledge from the forbidden tree and thereby lost access to the tree of life.

Let everyone who reads this acknowledge the Lord's righteousness.

If God sees fit to set aside even useful and prosperous people, like broken vessels, and raises up others to take their place, they should willingly lay aside worldly concerns and devote their remaining days to preparing for death.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.26.1-2Chr.26.15]
Chapter 26
Chapter Outline
Uzziah's good reign in Judah. | (1-15) |
Uzziah's attempt to burn incense. | (16-23) |
Verses 1-15
As long as Uzziah sought the Lord, and minded religion, God made him to prosper. Those only prosper whom God makes to prosper; for prosperity is his gift. Many have owned, that as long as they sought the Lord, and kept close to their duty, they prospered; but when they forsook God, every thing went cross. God never continues either to bless the indolent or to withhold his blessing from the diligent. He will never suffer any to seek his face in vain. Uzziah's name was famed throughout all the neighbouring countries. A name with God and good people makes truly honourable. He did not delight in war, nor addict himself to sports, but delighted in husbandry.
[2Chr.26.16-2Chr.26.23]
Verses 16-23
The transgression of the kings before Uzziah was, forsaking the temple of the Lord, and burning incense upon idolatrous altars. But his transgression was, going into the holy place, and attempting to burn incense upon the altar of God. See how hard it is to avoid one extreme, and not run into another. Pride of heart was at the bottom of his sin; a lust that ruins many. Instead of lifting up the name God in gratitude to him who had done so much for him, his heart was lifted up to his hurt. Men's pretending to forbidden knowledge, and seeking things too high for them, are owing to pride of heart. The incense of our prayers must be, by faith, put into the hands of our Lord Jesus, the great High Priest of our profession, else we cannot expect it to be accepted by God, [Rev.8.3] Re 8:3. Though Uzziah strove with the priests, he would not strive with his Maker. But he was punished for his transgression; he continued a leper to his death, shut out from society. The punishment answered the sin as face to face in a glass. Pride was at the bottom of his transgression, and thus God humbled him, and put dishonour upon him. Those that covet forbidden honours, forfeit allowed ones. Adam, by catching at the tree of knowledge which he might not eat of, debarred himself of the tree of life which he might have eaten of. Let all that read say, The Lord is righteous. And when the Lord sees good to throw prosperous and useful men aside, as broken vessels, if he raises up others to fill their places, they may rejoice to renounce all worldly concerns, and employ their remaining days in preparation for death.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Jotham's reign in Judah.

Jotham's reign

The people continued acting corruptly.

Perhaps Jotham did not do all he could to reform the land.

Even a very good person may lack the courage and zeal to perform duties that are within reach.

The people's own conduct certainly deserved blame.

Jotham prospered and became powerful.

The more steadfastly we follow God, the stronger we become—both in resisting evil and in doing good.

The Lord often removes wise and devout rulers and gives a people others whose folly and wickedness punish them for having failed to appreciate earlier blessings.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.27.1]
Chapter 27
Jotham's reign in Judah.
--The people did corruptly. Perhaps Jotham was wanting towards the reformation of the land. Men may be very good, and yet not have courage and zeal to do what they might. It certainly casts blame upon the people. Jotham prospered, and became mighty. The more stedfast we are in religion, the more mighty we are, both to resist evil, and to do good. The Lord often removes wise and pious rulers, and sends others, whose follies and vices punish a people that valued not their mercies.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The wicked reign of Ahaz in Judah.

Ahaz's wicked reign

Israel defeated Judah because the Lord was angry with Judah and used the northern kingdom as an instrument of his judgment.

Yet he also reminded Israel of its own sins.

Sinners have no right to act cruelly toward others.

How could they expect God's mercy if they refused mercy and justice to their brothers?

Remember that every human being is our neighbor and fellow human being, even when not a fellow Christian.

Henry makes an explicit statement here: anyone who knows God's word should be able to maintain confidently that slavery is contrary to the law of love and the gospel of grace.

How can someone hold a brother in bondage without breaking the rule to treat others as one would wish to be treated?

When sinners are abandoned to their own sinful desires, however, they grow more desperate in evil.

God commanded the Israelites to release the captives, and they obeyed.

The Lord brought Judah low.

People who refuse to humble themselves under God's word will rightly be humbled by his judgments.

Wicked people often have no real love for those who abandon true faith to join them, nor any desire to help them.

Ahaz became worse, not better, because of his suffering.

In distress he continued sinning more and set his heart even more firmly on wrongdoing.

When people misunderstand both the source of their troubles and the source of help, they turn their loyalties toward the wrong objects.

Wickedness and misery may grow rapidly together.

It is dreadful to consider a sinner dying and entering eternity while still hardened in sin.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.28.1]
Chapter 28
The wicked reign of Ahaz in Judah.
--Israel gained this victory because God was wroth with Judah, and made them the rod of his indignation. He reminds them of their own sins. It ill becomes sinners to be cruel. Could they hope for the mercy of God, if they neither showed mercy nor justice to their brethren? Let it be remembered, that every man is our neighbour, our brother, our fellow man, if not our fellow Christian. And no man who is acquainted with the word of God, need fear to maintain that slavery is against the law of love and the gospel of grace. Who can hold his brother in bondage, without breaking the rule of doing to others as he would they should do unto him? But when sinners are left to their own heart's lusts, they grow more desperate in wickedness. God commands them to release the prisoners, and they obeyed. The Lord brought Judah low. Those who will not humble themselves under the word of God, will justly be humbled by his judgments. It is often found, that wicked men themselves have no real affection for those that revolt to them, nor do they care to do them a kindness. This is that king Ahaz! that wretched man! Those are wicked and vile indeed, that are made worse by their afflictions, instead of being made better by them; who, in their distress, trespass yet more, and have their hearts more fully set in them to do evil. But no marvel that men's affections and devotions are misplaced, when they mistake the author of their trouble and of their help. The progress of wickedness and misery is often rapid; and it is awful to reflect upon a sinner's being driven away in his wickedness into the eternal world.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesHezekiah's good reign in Judah.1–19Hezekiah's sacrifice of atonement.20–36
Hezekiah begins reform (verses 1–19)

As soon as Hezekiah became king, he began to reform Judah's worship.

Those who begin their work with God begin at the right place, and he can bless their efforts.

Turning away from God's appointed worship is genuinely a way of turning away from God himself.

People still neglect true worship if Scripture is not read and explained, pictured by lighting the temple lamps, or if prayer and praise are not offered, pictured by burning incense.

Neglect of worship had caused the troubles Judah had endured.

Only the Lord can prepare a human heart for living faith.

When much good is accomplished quickly, all the glory belongs to him.

Those who love God and care about people's souls will rejoice.

Everyone who does good work should seek to do it well.

The offerings of atonement (verses 20–36)

When Hezekiah learned the temple was ready, he acted at once.

The sins of the preceding reign required atonement.

Mourning over sin and abandoning it were not enough; the people also brought a sin offering.

Likewise, our repentance and reform do not themselves earn pardon.

Forgiveness is available only through Jesus Christ, who became sin—that is, a sin offering—for us.

While the offerings burned, the Levites sang.

Grief over sin must never prevent us from praising God.

The king and congregation consented to the proceedings.

Merely being present where others worship is not enough.

We must worship God with our own hearts.

Our spiritual sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving should be accompanied by giving ourselves and everything we possess to God.

These sacrifices become acceptable to the Father only through the Redeemer.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.29.1-2Chr.29.19]
Chapter 29
Chapter Outline
Hezekiah's good reign in Judah. | (1-19) |
Hezekiah's sacrifice of atonement. | (20-36) |
Verses 1-19
When Hezekiah came to the crown, he applied at once to work reform. Those who begin with God, begin at the right end of their work, and it will prosper accordingly. Those that turn their backs upon God's ordinances, may truly be said to forsake God himself. There are still such neglects, if the word be not duly read and opened, for that was signified by the lighting the lamps, and also if prayers and praise be not offered up, for that was signified by the burning incense. Neglect of God's worship was the cause of the calamities they had lain under. The Lord alone can prepare the heart of man for vital godliness: when much good is done in a little time, the glory must be ascribed to him; and all who love him or the souls of men, will rejoice therein. Let those that do good work, learn to do it well.
[2Chr.29.20-2Chr.29.36]
Verses 20-36
As soon as Hezekiah heard that the temple was ready, he lost no time. Atonement must be made for the sins of the last reign. It was not enough to lament and forsake those sins; they brought a sin-offering. Our repentance and reformation will not obtain pardon but in and through Christ, who was made sin, that is, a sin-offering for us. While the offerings were on the altar, the Levites sang. Sorrow for sin must not prevent us from praising God. The king and the congregation gave their consent to all that was done. It is not enough for us to be where God is worshipped, if we do not ourselves worship with the heart. And we should offer up our spiritual sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving, and devote ourselves and all we have, as sacrifices, acceptable to the Father only through the Redeemer.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesHezekiah's passover.1–12The passover celebrated.13–20The feast of unleavened bread.21–27
Hezekiah invites all Israel to the Passover (verses 1–12)

Hezekiah made the Israelites from the northern kingdom as welcome to the Passover as his own subjects.

Let us give ourselves to the Lord.

Instead of insisting on doing what pleases us, resolve to do what pleases him.

Our fallen minds are naturally stubborn and unwilling to comply with God's ways.

We have inherited that disposition from our ancestors, and it must be overcome.

People whom grace has turned to God should do everything they can to bring others to him.

Many will mock the invitation.

Yet some will be humbled and blessed, perhaps where we least expect it.

God's rich mercy is the strongest reason for calling sinners to repentance.

Even the worst sinners who humble themselves before the Lord, seek his grace and devote themselves to his service can be saved.

How wonderful it would be if messengers went through every city, village and country with this good news!

The Passover is celebrated (verses 13–20)

The essential thing in attending God's solemn worship is a heart sincerely directed toward him.

Without this, everything else is worthless.

Even with a sincere, settled heart, worshipers may fall short of some sanctuary purification requirements.

Those defects need God's pardoning and healing grace.

Failing within a duty can be sinful, just as failing to perform the duty at all can be sinful.

If God judged even our best acts by the strict standard of his justice, we would be condemned.

Forgiveness must be sought through prayer, through the blood of Christ.

Every defect is cause for humility and repentance, not for despair.

But nothing can replace a heart prepared to seek the Lord.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread (verses 21–27)

Many prayers accompanied the fellowship offerings.

In these prayers the people recognized the Lord as the God of their fathers, their covenant God.

There was also much faithful preaching.

The Levites read and explained the Scriptures.

Faith comes through hearing, and true religion has often flourished when preaching was abundant.

The people sang psalms every day.

Praising God should occupy a large place in our gatherings.

After observing the feast for seven days, they found such joy in worship that they continued for another seven days.

They did so gladly.

Holy duties should be performed with holy joy.

When sinners humble themselves before the Lord, they can expect to rejoice in his appointed worship.

Those who taste that joy will not soon grow tired of it.

They will gladly prolong their time with God.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.30.1-2Chr.30.12]
Chapter 30
Chapter Outline
Hezekiah's passover. | (1-12) |
The passover celebrated. | (13-20) |
The feast of unleavened bread. | (21-27) |
Verses 1-12
Hezekiah made Israel as welcome to the passover, as any of his own subjects. Let us yield ourselves unto the Lord. Say not, you will do what you please, but resolve to do what he pleases. We perceive in the carnal mind a stiffness, an obstinacy, an unaptness to compel with God; we have it from our fathers: this must be overcome. Those who, through grace, have turned to God themselves, should do all they can to bring others to him. Numbers will be scorners, but some will be humbled and benefited; perhaps where least expected. The rich mercy of God is the great argument by which to enforce repentance; the vilest who submit and yield themselves to the Lord, seek his grace, and give themselves to his service, shall certainly be saved. Oh that messengers were sent forth to carry these glad tidings to every city and every village, through every land!
[2Chr.30.13-2Chr.30.20]
Verses 13-20
The great thing needful in attendance upon God in solemn ordinances, is, that we make heart-work of it; all is nothing without this. Where this sincerity and fixedness of heart are, there may yet be many things short of the purification of the sanctuary. These defects need pardoning, healing grace; for omissions in duty are sins, as well as omissions of duty. If God should deal with us in strict justice, even as to the very best of our doings, we should be undone. The way to obtain pardon, is to seek it of God by prayer; it must be gotten by petition through the blood of Christ. Yet every defect is sin, and needs forgiveness; and should be matter to humble, but not to discourage us, though nothing can make up for the want of a heart prepared to seek the Lord.
[2Chr.30.21-2Chr.30.27]
Verses 21-27
Many prayers were put up to God with the peace-offerings. In these Israel looked to God as the God of their fathers, a God in covenant with them. There was also abundance of good preaching. The Levites read and explained the Scriptures. Faith cometh by hearing, and true religion preaching has abounded. They sang psalms every day: praising God should be much of our work in religious assemblies. Having kept the seven days of the feast in this religious manner, they had so much comfort in it, that they kept other seven days also. This they did with gladness. Holy duties should be done with holy gladness. And when sinners humble themselves before the Lord, they may expect gladness in his ordinances. Those who taste this happiness will not soon grow weary of it, but will be glad to prolong their enjoyment.
